Chapter 11

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions that tend to arrive just after the first explanation.

Some questions cross chapter boundaries. Here we bring those pieces back together.

Is MoQ a finished standard?

The baseline for this edition is draft-ietf-moq-transport-21, dated September 8, 2026. At the research date, it is an active Internet-Draft rather than a published RFC. Treat wire details as versioned and check the current IETF document status before implementing them.

This book is a dated explanation, not an automatically synchronized mirror of the specification. Links to the pinned draft preserve what the edition describes. Links to project documentation can change after publication.

Does MoQ replace WebRTC?

For a side-by-side introduction, start with How does MoQ compare with WebRTC?.

The two can serve some of the same applications. Consider our lecture: a conversation between the lecturer and a student, and delivery to a large listening audience, are different parts of the same experience. Either technology may be used in a larger system that supports both.

In a browser, WebRTC provides much of the encoding, transmission, and receiving machinery together. A MoQ implementation supplies named-content delivery; its media library supplies the capture, codec, and playback pieces above it. Compare complete systems on the devices and network paths your audience uses. The protocol name alone does not tell you the delay or operating cost.

Does it replace HLS or DASH?

HLS (HTTP Live Streaming) and DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) describe ways for players to obtain media in pieces over HTTP, the protocol used for web requests. A description of the available media tells the player which pieces to request. This fits established web servers and caching infrastructure. The DASH Industry Forum’s architecture overview describes DASH’s presentation description and segment model.

MoQ instead lets a receiver subscribe to a named track and receive objects as they become available. Both approaches need media formats, players, and a policy for adapting to the network. Neither the use of HTTP nor subscription by itself fixes the final playback delay. HLS’s playlist-and-segment model is described in RFC 8216, section 2; MoQ subscriptions are described in draft-21, section 3.1.

A service can use more than one delivery path. The moq.dev project includes gateways for established formats and protocols. A gateway is a concrete integration to test, not evidence that every arbitrary MoQ publication is playable by an HLS player.

Why would I cancel a reliable stream?

Reliability repairs missing bytes; it does not decide whether you still want them. Suppose the viewer has fallen behind and the player can restart from a newer, independently decodable group. Spending more time repairing an older group may prolong the delay. The delivery policy can stop that old work while retaining reliable delivery for work that is still useful.

The receiver also needs to discard its stale playback queue and resume at a valid point. Cancellation alone cannot make a player catch up. Latency and Congestion follows those decisions.

This also answers a common question: is all MoQ traffic unreliable? No. An active QUIC stream provides reliable, ordered bytes. Datagrams are a separate option: QUIC does not retransmit them when they are lost. QUIC and WebTransport explains the distinction.

Can I send chat or game state?

The payload model is not limited to media. But your data still needs a design that matches loss, ordering, and late joining. A fresh state snapshot can replace an old one. An isolated “increment score” event often cannot.

For an illustrative game, put a full state snapshot at a restart boundary and define how later updates relate to it. If you need an authoritative event history, provide persistence and recovery deliberately rather than assuming a live track is a database.

Is MoQ peer-to-peer?

MOQT can operate between endpoints or through relays. It does not by itself supply every rendezvous and NAT traversal mechanism needed for arbitrary browser-to-browser connectivity. The common browser deployment connects outward to a server through WebTransport.

Some native stacks add their own peer connectivity. Those are implementation capabilities to investigate separately from the core object and subscription model.

Is moq-lite the same as MOQT?

No. moq-lite uses a simpler model, and the moq.dev stack implements compatibility paths for specified MOQT versions. Compatibility depends on the negotiated revision, supported features, and media format. Two products carrying “MoQ” in their name are not an interoperability test.

Can I use this book as a specification?

Use it to understand the problems and vocabulary. Use the exact applicable protocol draft for normative behavior, and the documentation for the library version you ship. The walkthrough commands are sourced examples, not a claim that every supported platform was tested.
